newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks $3.9 billion rescue plan for capital.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks $3.9 billion rescue plan for capital.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday proposed a $3.9 billion, five-year plan to help rescue the District of Columbia government from fiscal crisis and prop up its crumbling infrastructure.
"This nation's capital city is in distress and it's important that the American people understand that, and understand what we are going to do about it," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.
He said the $3.9 billion plan would replace the federal government's annual $660 million payment to the district, representing a net gain of $339 million over the period.

Behind its tourist attractions -- the White House, the monuments and the museums -- Washington is a city of 543,000 people, many poor and black, which has lurched from crisis to crisis in recent years.

It is plagued by a high crime rate -- 19 homicides have already been recorded in the new year and many schools have metal-detectors to keep students from carrying guns inside. Streets are potholed and heavy snow last winter overwhelmed ill-equipped road crews.
"He (Clinton) wants to be a good neighbour, and he wants to live in a good neighbourhood," McCurry said.

The package would have the federal government help the district pay medical bills for its poorest citizens and would grant tax incentives for economic development at a time when many businesses are fleeing the city for smaller tax burdens in neighbouring Maryland and Virginia.

The new funds will also go toward prison renovation and construction, operation of prison facilities and courts, and a start to rebuilding the city's transportation infrastructure and improving its ability to collect taxes, McCurry said.

In essence, the federal government would be taking responsibility for billions of dollars in district programmes in exchange for eliminating the annual payment. McCurry said the plan was similar to the way U.S. state governments support their cities.

It was welcomed by the D.C. delegate to Congress, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Andrew Brimmer, chairman of a financial control board appointed to revamp the city government. Mayor Marion Barry also said he was encouraged by the move.

Senior U.S. officials were to unveil details of the plan later on Tuesday. It is to be included in Clinton's budget proposal for the 1998 fiscal year starting next Oct. 1, which he is to submit to Congress on Feb. 6.
Congress must approve the aid package.
